idiom_name: multiprocessing.Pool.map / concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor for the forks, recursion for the splits
implementation_notes: concurrent.futures gives the pool and the join: ProcessPoolExecutor.submit returns a Future whose result() joins, map/as_completed join a whole fan-out, and multiprocessing.Pool offers the same interface over processes - both sidestep the GIL, which matters because a CPU-bound leaf in a thread still serialises. The recursion itself stays ordinary Python (slicing and a plain loop at the base case); the pool replaces the classic task pool, and leaves should be coarse because every argument and result crossing the process boundary is pickled. Use ThreadPoolExecutor only when the leaf blocks on I/O.
code_sketch:
def solve(chunk):
    if len(chunk) < 4096: return leaf(chunk)        # base case
    return merge(solve(chunk[:len(chunk)//2]),      # or submit the halves
                 solve(chunk[len(chunk)//2:]))

with multiprocessing.Pool() as pool:                # forks + joins, GIL-free
    parts = pool.map(apply_leaf, split_into_chunks(data))
return merge_all(parts)                             # combine
pitfalls: Everything crossing the process boundary is pickled: fine-grained decomposition loses to serialization, and lambdas or closures cannot be pickled at all.
The default start method is spawn on macOS/Windows, so the entry point needs the if __name__ == '__main__' guard or children re-import and re-fork.
A process pool cannot be nested inside a worker process (daemonic children may not have children): keep the fan-out one level deep.
